metaDescription: Five corded SDS-Plus rotary hammers under $200, compared on joules, weight, modes and the safety clutch that matters when a bit binds in rebar.
expertTake: The ENEACRO 12.5 amp with a 7 joule claim is the pick for anyone drilling real concrete, because it states its 7 joule blow energy plainly in the unit that matters. The Deshuo 9 amp is the value pick for ladder and overhead work, giving up impact energy for a body just over 7 pounds. If you only need a couple of anchor holes a year, rent a pro unit or buy a plain hammer drill, because an SDS tool is only worth owning when you buy the bits to go with it.
introParagraphs: An SDS-Plus rotary hammer is a corded machine that hits the back of a slotted bit with a piston, so the bit does the chipping while the tool does the turning. The listing numbers (amps, rpm, blows per minute) rarely agree with each other, and the one that predicts speed is often buried.

This guide explains what a spending cap of $200 buys in an SDS-Plus tool, what separates it from a pro unit, and which specs to trust. Our top picks are above and the full reviews follow. Prices move, and the cap reflects listing prices when this guide was updated.

products.name: ENEACRO 12.5 Amp 1-1/4 in SDS-Plus Rotary Hammer, 7J
products.description:
This ENEACRO model quotes 7 joules of impact energy, stated plainly in joules, from a 12.5 amp motor. Joules are the number that predicts concrete speed, because they measure how hard each piston stroke hits the bit, and 7 J puts the tool in the range that handles 3/4 inch anchor holes and 1-1/4 inch core bits without grinding to a stop.

It has three modes: drill only for wood and steel, hammer drill for concrete and chisel for light demolition. The tradeoff is the three-mode design, which lacks the fourth chisel-angle lock found on some rivals, so you cannot fix the chisel at a set angle. Against the ENEACRO ENRH3201 in this list, which is rated at 13 amps and 5.5 foot-pounds (about 7.5 J), the two land within a few percent on blow energy despite the amp gap, a good example of why amps are a poor guide.

The 360 degree adjustable side handle and anti-vibration design help with fatigue, and a safety clutch slips if the bit binds on rebar. Plan on greasing the chuck and clearing dust from the vents after each concrete job.
products.bestFor: Regular concrete anchors and holes up to 3/4 inch.
pros: 7 J is stated plainly in joules, the unit that predicts concrete speed
Adjustable 360 degree side handle improves control and comfort
Safety clutch slips when a bit binds on rebar
Drill-only mode doubles as a heavy-duty wood and steel drill
cons: Three modes, so no fixed chisel angle lock, and a heavier body than the 9 amp units
Heavier than the 9 amp units in this roundup

products.name: ENEACRO ENRH3201 13 Amp 1-1/4 in SDS-Plus Rotary Hammer
products.description:
The ENRH3201 carries a larger amp rating than its sibling but a lower impact figure at 5.5 foot-pounds, about 7.5 joules, so on paper the two ENEACRO units are close. The extra amps show up as more sustained power when you drill deep holes continuously, since a bigger motor stays cooler when it pushes a 1 inch bit through a 4 inch slab.

It offers four functions, including a vario-lock style chisel setting, which the 7 J unit lacks. The tradeoff is a slightly heavier body and a design that feels like a generic import rather than a polished pro tool. Compared with the DEKOPRO in this roundup, which is rated 12.5 amps with a 5.5 J claim, the ENRH3201 is nearly identical in class.

Buy a set of SDS-Plus bits, wear safety glasses and a dust mask, and check the carbon brushes after a few years of regular use. A little grease in the chuck keeps the bits sliding and the piston protected.
products.bestFor: Longer drilling sessions where a stronger motor stays cool.
pros: 13 amp motor handles deep holes with less heat build-up
Four functions include a lockable chisel setting

Heavier than the 9 amp rotary hammers

products.name: DEKOPRO 12.5 Amp 1-1/4 in SDS-Plus Rotary Hammer
products.description:
The DEKOPRO pairs a 12.5 amp motor with a 5.5 joule claim, no-load speeds of 0 to 1000 rpm and 0 to 4600 blows per minute, and a side selector that switches between four functions. Because the selector sits on the side of the tool, you can change mode without letting go of the trigger handle.

Compared with the Deshuo's 3 J, the DEKOPRO hits about 80 percent harder per blow, which is the difference between a 3/8 inch hole in one minute and a 3/4 inch hole in the same minute. Against the ENEACRO 7 J unit, it gives up roughly a quarter of the blow energy, but it has a fourth mode that the 7 J unit lacks.

The BPM figure is a no-load number and it drops under load, so do not judge speed by it. Keep the chuck greased, buy quality SDS-Plus bits and expect to replace carbon brushes after a few years of concrete work.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want four modes and solid energy at a low price tier.
pros: 5.5 J is about 80 percent stronger per blow than the 3 J units
Side selector changes modes without releasing the handle
Four functions cover drilling, hammering and chiseling
Safety clutch limits kickback if the bit binds
cons: Impact energy trails the 7 J ENEACRO
No-load BPM figure drops under load

products.name: Deshuo 9 Amp 1 in SDS-Plus Lightweight Rotary Hammer
products.description:
At 7.19 pounds the Deshuo is the lightest rotary hammer in this roundup, and the weight is the whole point. Drilling overhead into a ceiling slab with a 10 pound tool is tiring, and a lighter tool lets you hold the bit square for longer. The motor is 9 amps with 3 joules of impact energy, so it is sized for 1/4 to 1/2 inch anchors, with a stated maximum of 1 inch.

It gives up power to get there. Compared with the ENEACRO 7 J unit, it delivers less than half the blow energy, so each hole takes longer, and a 3/4 inch hole in cured concrete is a slow job. The listing warns it works only with SDS-Plus bits, not SDS-Max or standard drills.

It is a sensible tool for electricians and installers who drill small holes overhead all day. Clean the chuck, keep the vents clear and replace carbon brushes when power fades. Overhead work also benefits from a dust shroud or a helper holding a vacuum, because concrete dust falls straight onto your face.
products.bestFor: Overhead and ladder work with small anchors.

products.name: WORKPRO 7.5 Amp 1-1/4 in SDS-Plus Rotary Hammer Kit
products.description:
WORKPRO sells this tool as a kit: a 7.5 amp rotary hammer with four functions, a 360 degree rotatable handle and five SDS-Plus bits in the box. The bits matter, because a first-time buyer otherwise has to purchase a set before drilling a single hole, and bundled bits get you started on day one.

The 7.5 amp motor is the weakest in the group, so the tool is suited to 1/4 to 1/2 inch anchors and occasional tapcons, not the 1 inch holes the 1-1/4 inch label suggests. Compared with the Deshuo's 9 amps and 3 joules, it has less motor but a wider mode selection and the bundled bits. Against the DEKOPRO, it gives up roughly 40 percent of the amp rating.

The maker says the structure passes a one meter drop test, a durability claim worth treating as a manufacturer statement. Keep the bits clean and replace them when the carbide tips round off. If the listing's drop-test claim matters to you, treat it as a seller statement rather than a rating.

buyingCriteria.explanation: Amps describe how much current the motor draws and joules describe how hard each blow hits, and the second predicts concrete speed. The ENEACRO 12.5 amp claims 7 J, the DEKOPRO claims 5.5 J and the Deshuo claims 3 J. A common mistake is buying the highest amp number and expecting a faster tool, when the ENRH3201's 13 amps and the 12.5 amp unit's 7 J claim land within a few percent of each other on blow energy.

A heavier rotary hammer drills better because the mass helps the piston, but it tires your arms. The Deshuo weighs 7.19 pounds, and the larger 12 to 13 amp units are heavier. If you drill upward more than a few holes, lighter is better, and if you work on floors, heavier tools win.

Four-mode tools add a lockable chisel position so you can set the chisel at a fixed angle, which a three-mode tool cannot. The DEKOPRO, ENRH3201 and WORKPRO offer four functions, while the 7 J ENEACRO has three. Chiseling is a bonus feature for light tile and mortar removal, not a replacement for a demolition hammer.

When a bit snags rebar, the tool wants to spin in your hands. A safety clutch slips at a set torque to protect your wrists, and a side handle lets you brace the tool. The ENEACRO units and the DEKOPRO list a safety clutch, and the WORKPRO and ENEACRO 7 J have a rotatable 360 degree handle.

SDS-Plus bits only fit SDS-Plus chucks, and SDS-Max tools are different. Bits are a real part of the cost, since a decent set of carbide-tip bits can cost as much as a bargain tool. The WORKPRO includes five bits, which helps a first-time buyer, while the others need a separate set.

Corded tools need a heavy-gauge extension cord, since a thin cord loses voltage and overheats the motor. A 9 amp tool like the Deshuo is easier on a cord than a 13 amp tool like the ENRH3201. Use a 12 gauge cord for runs beyond 50 feet.

specDecoder.meaning: Joules measure the energy of one piston blow. Higher joules chip concrete faster and allow larger holes.
specDecoder.watchFor: The ENRH3201 quotes ft-lbs while the other ENEACRO quotes joules, and 5.5 ft-lbs is about 7.5 J, so convert before ranking them.

specDecoder.meaning: Blows per minute is the strike rate at no load. It falls under load and is only meaningful alongside joules.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Deshuo's 0 to 5300 BPM beats the DEKOPRO's 4600 but hits with less than 60 percent of the energy.

specDecoder.meaning: Amps are current draw, which indicates motor size but not efficiency. A bigger motor stays cooler under sustained load.
specDecoder.watchFor: Do not treat the WORKPRO's 7.5 amps and the ENRH3201's 13 amps as a 2 to 1 performance gap.

specDecoder.meaning: The largest bit diameter the tool is rated to drill in concrete. It assumes a good bit and a firm hand.
specDecoder.watchFor: The WORKPRO lists a 1-1/4 inch label with a 7.5 amp motor, which is optimistic.

specDecoder.meaning: A 10 mm bit shank with slots that lock into the chuck while allowing it to slide. This sliding is what lets the piston strike the bit directly.
specDecoder.watchFor: SDS-Plus bits will not fit SDS-Max tools.

howWeEvaluated.title: Impact energy
howWeEvaluated.description: We converted every listing to joules before comparing, since 5.5 ft-lbs is about 7.5 J. The ENEACRO 12.5 amp at 7 J and the ENRH3201 at about 7.5 J were effectively tied at the top, followed by the DEKOPRO at 5.5 J, with the Deshuo at 3 J and the WORKPRO unstated.

howWeEvaluated.title: Weight and handling
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared body weight and handle design. The Deshuo at 7.19 pounds was the lightest, and the WORKPRO and ENEACRO 7 J scored for their 360 degree handles.

howWeEvaluated.title: Modes and safety
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at the number of functions and whether a safety clutch was listed. The four-function units scored above the three-mode ENEACRO 7 J.

howWeEvaluated.title: Kit contents
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered what is in the box. The WORKPRO includes five bits, and the others require a separate SDS-Plus set.

howWeEvaluated.title: Owner feedback patterns
howWeEvaluated.description: We noted recurring owner themes around brushes, chuck wear and bit quality rather than manufacturers' claims. Lesser known labels were scored cautiously on parts support.

cards.label: Light (Deshuo, WORKPRO)
cards.text: The Deshuo at 7.19 pounds and the WORKPRO suit overhead drilling, ladders and small anchors. They hit with less energy and take longer on bigger holes.

cards.label: Heavy (ENEACRO, DEKOPRO)
cards.text: The ENEACRO units and the DEKOPRO weigh more and hit harder, handling 3/4 inch holes and deeper drilling. They tire your arms on overhead jobs.

howToChoose.note: Pick light if most of your holes are overhead and small. Pick heavy if you drill floors and walls with larger bits.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: At least 3 J of impact energy, a depth stop and a side handle. Use carbide-tipped bits and blow dust from each hole before setting the anchor.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The ENEACRO 7 J unit and the DEKOPRO suit 3/8 to 3/4 inch anchors. The Deshuo and WORKPRO suit smaller anchors.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You drill concrete weekly or need a longer service life. A branded SDS-Plus unit outlasts the ENEACRO and DEKOPRO models.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You only drill a handful of anchors per year. The WORKPRO kit or the Deshuo does that job.

maintenance.why: SDS tools run on grease. Without it, the bit shank and piston wear faster, and a dry chuck is the usual reason a budget unit dies early.
Concrete dust works into the chuck. A torn boot lets dust in and wears the mechanism.
Worn brushes cause weak power and sparking. Replace them in pairs.
Rounded carbide tips slow the tool and overheat it. Replace worn bits.
A nicked cord is a shock hazard. Replace it before use.

faq.q: Do I need an SDS-Plus tool or a regular hammer drill?
faq.a: An SDS-Plus tool drills concrete far faster, but it needs SDS bits. For a few holes a year, a regular hammer drill is enough.

faq.q: What does $200 buy in an SDS-Plus hammer?
faq.a: A corded 7.5 to 13 amp tool with roughly 3 to 7.5 joules of stated impact energy. You give up the brand support, refined vibration control and metal gear cases of a pro unit, and you will need to budget for decent SDS-Plus bits. The cap reflects listing prices when this guide was updated.

faq.q: How long should an SDS-Plus tool last?
faq.a: With light household use, many years, since the mechanism is simple and sealed in grease. Heavy daily use wears the brushes and the chuck mechanism much faster, and the lesser known labels may be hard to service.

faq.q: Are joules or amps the better measure?
faq.a: Joules, because they measure blow energy. Amps only show current draw.

faq.q: Can I use an SDS-Plus tool as a regular drill?
faq.a: Yes, in drill-only mode with an SDS-Plus adapter chuck, though most tools are used with SDS bits. Check that your tool has a drill-only mode.
Yes. Wear safety glasses, hearing protection and a dust mask, since concrete dust is a respiratory hazard.
